To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

microcredit interest rates can be lower than those of traditional moneylenders because microcredit is more efficient at screening borrowers and monitoring repayment, and that microcredit interest rate can be higher than that of commercial banks because microcredit is a substitute for collateral.

(i) microcredit is a substitute for traditional moneylending; (ii) the interest rates charged by microcredit are lower than those charged by traditional money-lenders, but higher for commercial banks; (iii) microcredit interest rates have been declining over time, as microcredit institutions have gained market share; and (iv) microcredit interest rate differentials have declined over time, but are still significant.

microcredit interest rates can be explained by the discontinuous nature of the marginal revenue curve for microcredit, the U-shaped supply curve for capital, and the fact that the supply of capital is constrained by the lack of complementary human and financial capital, and by transaction costs for the small loan sizes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the microcredit industry and the role that microcredit plays in developing economies.
the economics of the microcredit market, and the factors that explain the growth of microfinance and the decline in interest rates.
the economics of microcredit and how the supply of capital and the interest rate is determined in this environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
microcredit has overcome the barriers to capital flows, and the interest rates reflect the costs of doing business in the microcredit environment.
the microcredit industry has overcome these constraints through a variety of mechanisms.
microcredit has not overcome all of the barriers to capital flows, and that microcredit interest rates have not converged with those of commercial banks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

microcredit interest rates can be explained by the discontinuous nature of the marginal revenue curve and by the supply curve of capital, both in microfinance and in the traditional moneylending environment.

the interest rate is the result of the interplay of the demand for microfinance and the supply of capital, and that the interest rate reflects the cost of capital and the cost of the complementary human capital and information.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the economic and behavioral factors that constrain microcredit capital flows can be overcome with the right policy and institutional framework.
a discontinuous marginal cost curve for capital and the presence of a U-shaped capital supply curve for microcredit can explain the behavior of microcredit capital flows and interest rate.
the economic environment of the microcredit sector is different from that of the commercial banking sector and that this difference is crucial to understand the microcredit sector.
